prime.problem: Some models don't fit on one chip, and some users need lower latency than one chip's bandwidth allows. Training taught four ways to split a model, but three of them are useless or harmful in decode, and the one that works can be pushed much further than training allows. Pick wrong and you get an order-of-magnitude regression.
prime.fits: Tenth card, the start of Distributing inference. It reuses Bcrit and the step-time formula to decide how prefill and generation should be sharded, and it sets up the next card's question of where the KV cache goes.
expect: why not FSDP, data or sequence parallelism in decode
prime.goal: Choose a sharding for prefill and for generation, justify it from the roofline, and compute how far model parallelism can go before communication becomes the bottleneck.

attend: Why can prefill borrow all of training's sharding strategies while generation can't?
What exactly does FSDP move every step, and why is that fatal in decode but fine in training?
Why does data parallelism add throughput but not per-user speed?
In training, model sharding is limited by math vs communication. What is it compared against in decode, and why does that allow many more chips?
How does the Megatron split let the weights stay put while only small activations move?

must: Prefill is big compute-bound matmuls → it behaves like training → model sharding up to the point comms beat math (Y < F·W<sub>link</sub>/C ≈ F/2200, 4–8 way), then sequence parallelism for long prompts

Decode is bound by reading weights from HBM, and chip links are far slower than HBM → move activations, never weights → FSDP (gathering weights every step) costs 31.2 ms vs 4.8 ms for Llama-3.1-8B on 8 H100s → an order-of-magnitude regression

Data parallelism replicates the weights → each copy still reads all of them per step → adds throughput, not per-user speed; sequence sharding needs a sequence, and decode has one new token → only model parallelism is left

With Y-way model sharding each chip reads 1/Y of the weights (2DF/(Y·W<sub>hbm</sub>)) while activations cost 2BD/W<sub>ici</sub> → comms win only past Y > F/(B·β) → at small B that allows far more chips (64-way in the book's example) → more sharding buys latency at small batch
elevated: Megatron cuts the first MLP matrix by columns and the second by rows with the same hidden slice → the elementwise activation needs no talk → one all-reduce finishes the layer → two all-reduces per Transformer layer (after attention, after MLP)
KV weights are small (a quarter of Q + O for Llama-3.1-8B) → replicating them is cheaper than splitting past K heads → at 8-way TP each GPU gets exactly one of Llama's 8 KV heads
reference: β ≈ 8 on v5e/v6e (9.1 by arithmetic), 7.4 on H100 (9.1 at 370 GB/s)
F / 2200 in a node, F / 2475 beyond, F / 1995 in one answer

compress.prompt: Draw a 4 × 2 grid from memory: rows are model, data, FSDP and sequence parallelism; columns are prefill and generation. Mark each cell ✓ or ✗ with a five-word reason. Then write the two limits (prefill, generation) and say in one sentence why the second allows more chips.
checklist: prefill: model sharding first, then sequence; FSDP and pipelining viable
generation: only model parallelism; FSDP, data and sequence are out
prefill limit Y < F/2200 (comms vs math)
generation limit Y < F/(B·β) (comms vs weight read)
at small B the weight read is huge compared with activations, so more chips help latency

retrieve.q: Explain why leaving FSDP on after training is an order-of-magnitude regression at inference, in terms of what crosses the chip links each step.
answer: FSDP gathers each layer's weights from other chips just before running it
in decode that's nearly the whole model every step: 16.06 GB × 7/8 over 450 GB/s = 31.2 ms
reading the weights from local HBM takes 4.8 ms, so FSDP is ≈ 6.5× slower here and far worse with larger models or slower links

retrieve.q: Walk through one Megatron-sharded MLP on 4 devices: what each device holds, what it computes, and the one communication step.
answer: each device holds a column slice of W<sub>in</sub> (gate and up for SwiGLU) and the matching row slice of W<sub>out</sub>
each computes its slice of the hidden units and applies the activation locally
each multiplies by its W<sub>out</sub> rows to get a full-size partial output
one all-reduce sums the partials; the lab's sum matches unsharded to 2.22e-15

retrieve.q: Llama-3.1-8B fits on one H100 with room to spare. When is 8-way tensor parallelism for decode worth it, and when should you run 8 separate replicas instead?
answer: TP when you need per-token latency below one GPU's 4.8 ms weight-read floor: 8-way cuts it to 599 µs
replicas when throughput per GPU is the goal: no comms, no 64 all-reduces per step with fixed start-up costs
at large batch near B<sub>crit</sub>, extra TP ways cost throughput per chip, so throughput-first serving stops at F/α

compare.q: This card uses the Megatron split as a given; the Megatron card walks the paper. Why is the column-then-row pairing, rather than two column splits, the reason only one all-reduce is needed per MLP?
answer: column-splitting the first matrix leaves each device with a full-row slice of hidden units, on which the activation is local
row-splitting the second matrix consumes exactly that slice and produces a partial sum of the full output
two column splits would need an all-gather of the hidden activations in between, adding a collective

compare.q: FSDP is a win in training and a regression in decode. What is it trading in each case, and which quantity flips the verdict?
answer: it trades memory (each chip stores 1/N of the weights) for gathering them before each layer
in training, big batches give each layer enough math to hide the gathers
in decode, the batch is small and the step is already bound by moving weights, so the gathers over slower links become the whole step

predict.q: LLaMA 3-70B (F = 28,672) on an 8×H100 node, β = 7.44. Commit first: at batch 32, is 8-way TP comfortably inside the generation limit? At batch 256, roughly where does the limit fall?
predict.answer: Y* = F/(B·β): at B = 32 it is 28,672/(32 × 7.44) ≈ 120, so 8-way is far inside. At B = 256 it is ≈ 15, still above 8. The whole-step estimate agrees: at B = 256 and 8-way, weights take 5.22 ms per GPU, math 4.53 ms and the all-reduces about 2.6 ms at 450 GB/s, so the weight read still dominates. Doubling F doubled Y*, as the card's try-this says.

apply.task: Adapt labs/sharding-prefill-generation.py part (b2) to LLaMA 3-70B on 8×H100 (140 GB bf16, D = 8,192, F = 28,672, 80 layers, so 160 all-reduces per step). For B = 32 and B = 256 at 8-way TP, compute Tweights, Tmath and Tcomm at 450 GB/s, and the book's Y* at both batches. State the bottleneck in each case and the prefill limit F/2200.
apply.done: You find T<sub>weights</sub> ≈ 5.22 ms in both cases; at B = 32, T<sub>math</sub> ≈ 0.57 ms and T<sub>comm</sub> ≈ 0.33 ms; at B = 256, ≈ 4.53 ms and ≈ 2.61 ms; Y* ≈ 120 and ≈ 15; prefill limit ≈ 13 ways. Weights are the bottleneck in both.

reflect: Which prediction did you get wrong: how far inside the limit 8-way sits for 70B?
Could you explain to a colleague why data parallelism doesn't help one user, in one sentence?
Which relationship is still fuzzy: small B → comms vs weight read → more chips allowed, or large B → back to the F/α limit?
Did the FSDP number surprise you? What would it be for a 70B model?
Before the next card: with 8 KV heads and 16 chips, where would you put the KV cache?
